name: Quilt Museum
character: Quiet institutional serif on heritage indigo: collection-led, visiting information up front, supporter levels instead of guild dues.

sections.title: {{guild_name}}
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Four centuries of American quilts, three exhibitions a year, and a study room open to any researcher with a question.

sections.heading: Visit
sections.when: Tuesday to Saturday, 10 to 5; Sunday, 12 to 4
sections.note: Admission is free on first Fridays. The study room is open by appointment for close looking.

sections.heading: Why quilts belong in a museum
sections.html:
A quilt is a document. It records the cloth that was available, the hours a family could spare, and the hands that held the needle. Collected and cared for, it outlasts the drawer it was folded into.

The center holds six hundred quilts, dated 1790 to the present, in a climate-controlled vault. Conservation is ongoing and visible: the workroom window looks onto the framing bench.

sections.title: Become a supporter
sections.body: Supporter levels fund conservation framing and the school program. Members visit free all year.

sections.title: The collection
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Six hundred quilts and four generations of generous donors, from whole-cloth linseys to art quilts of the last decade.

sections.heading: Studying a quilt up close
sections.html: The study room seats twelve and any quilt in the vault can be requested by catalog number. Appointments are Tuesday and Thursday mornings; bring pencils only, and cotton gloves are provided.

sections.title: Exhibitions
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Three curated shows a year, plus one open-wall weekend when any quilt in the county may hang.

sections.heading: The archive
sections.html: Past exhibitions stay on view as online albums, with the curator's notes and the label copy for every quilt. Ten years of catalogs are available in the reading room.

sections.title: Plan your visit
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Hours, directions, parking, and what to expect in the galleries.

sections.heading: Hours and directions
sections.when: Tuesday to Saturday, 10 to 5; Sunday, 12 to 4
sections.note: Two hours from New York by Amtrak; the station is a ten-minute walk.

sections.heading: Groups and accessibility
sections.html:
Guild bus trips and school groups are welcome, with a docent if booked two weeks ahead. The galleries are on one level, wheelchairs are available at the desk, and the reading room has a large-print catalog.

Photography without flash is encouraged, except where a label asks otherwise; loans from private collectors sometimes travel with that condition.

items.q: Is the museum suitable for children?
items.a: Yes. The scavenger hunt card keeps young visitors moving, and the hands-on quilting frame in the lobby is for everyone.

items.q: How long does a visit take?
items.a: About an hour for the galleries. The study room appointment is separate and lasts as long as your questions do.

items.q: Can I donate a quilt to the collection?
items.a: Please write first with photographs and what you know of its history. The collections committee meets quarterly.

sections.title: Support the center
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Supporter memberships, conservation adoption, and the autumn benefit auction keep the vault cool and the lights on.

sections.heading: Where the money goes
sections.html: Membership underwrites the school program, which brings every fourth-grade class in the county through the galleries each spring. Conservation adoption covers the exact cost of stabilizing one quilt: batting, cloth, a conservator's hours, and a frame that will outlast us.

sections.title: Members visit free, all year
sections.body: Join today and your first exhibition opening invitation arrives this month.

sections.title: About {{guild_name}}
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Founded by two collectors and a borrowed exhibition wall, now the caretaker of six hundred quilts.

sections.heading: How the center began
sections.html:
The first exhibition hung in a bank lobby that stood empty after a merger: forty quilts, borrowed from attics, with hand-lettered labels. The lobby is a gallery now, the attic quilts mostly came back with thank-you notes, and a few never left.

The center is a not-for-profit governed by a board of nine, staffed by four full-time and a rotation of volunteers who know where the tissue paper lives.
